newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway, U.S. end Cold War arms agreement.
newsitem.headline: Norway, U.S. end Cold War arms agreement.

text.p: Norway and the United States formally ended a Cold War military assistance programme on Friday with Oslo paying Washington a token $1.8 million for equipment worth many times more.
The termination agreement was signed by Norwegian Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo and U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry the day after an annual NATO meeting in Bergen.
"Today we mark the end of nearly 50 years of military assistance cooperation between Norway and the United States," Perry said at a news conference.

Kosmo said NATO member Norway would never have been able to build up a strong defence had it not been for the assistance programme under which the country borrowed military equipment from the United States.
"The amount now paid back is just a symbolic sum," he said.
Officials said Norway was paying the scrap value of the equipment received in gaining the right to its residual value.
The hardware included 8,000 combat and transport vehicles, 500 pieces of artillery, 170,000 small arms, dozens of warships and more than 600 planes and helicopters.
Norwegian defence monthly Forsvarets Forum said the equipment was worth more than $12 billion in today's money.

The shipments ran from 1950 to 1971, but the bureaucracy involved in administering the borrowed material in the end proved a burden to both countries. For example, U.S. consent was necessary for the scrapping or selling of material received.
Perry and Kosmo agreed that both sides had benefited from the defence capabilities of Norway, which shares a border with Russia on what used to be the strategically-important Northern Flank.

U.S. Ambassador to Norway Thomas Loftus said Norway was the first country to settle its arms assistance bill with the United States, which had similar programmes in support of the defences of all NATO countries plus Japan, Thailand and the Philippines.
"Norway has set the standard," he said. "Now we must finish with the Cold War and the arms assistance programmes, so that we really can look to the future."
Perry said the termination of the agreement did not affect U.S. military equipment pre-positioned in mid-Norway in the 1980s for a possible Northern Flank conflict.
